newsitem.title: USA: Mass. legislators to take up bond issues this week.
newsitem.headline: Mass. legislators to take up bond issues this week.

text.p: Massachusetts legislators are expected this week to consider whether to override vetoes Gov. William Weld made in the huge transportation bond bill before he went on vacation Friday.

The commonwealth's transportation network will get a $3.9 billion infusion of money over the next two years under terms of the bond authorization. The combination of state and federal dollars will be used for road and mass transit projects.

But the question of how much money the government will chip in for the massive Central Artery project remains up in the air. Because of the uncertainty, the House and Senate included language in the bill that fees to renew driver's licenses and auto registrations will be reinstated if Washington decides to contribute less than $550 million a year to the project.

Weld considers elimination of those fees one of his proudest accomplishments, and vetoed the provision. A two-thirds vote in both branches is necessary to override that veto and put the language into effect.
Weld last week also made an interesting move on a bill providing $685 million over the next several years to upgrade the state's courthouses. The last such bond authorization came in 1988.

In recent years, many aging state and county courthouses have fallen into serious disrepair. The bond authorization promises new or improved facilities in 30 communities. But Weld returned the bill to lawmakers with recommendation that they strike a proviso stipulating only union laborers can be used on projects to rehabilitate existing courthouses or build new ones.

The House and Senate are expected to vote on the governor's recommendation. If the bill is re-enacted as is, with the governor's recommendation rejected, Weld is free to veto the section or sections to which he objects.

But, as with all other legislation, the governor will do so with the knowledge that his party is outnumbered 6 to 1 in the Legislature, and Democratic leadership has the power to override virtually any veto.
